title: Household fraud exposure separates into direct loss, recovery failure, and substantial time cost
source_unit: Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking adult respondent, 2024

denominator.unit: weighted adult population estimate; publication percentages are the denominator frame

non_credit_card_fraud_lost_money.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

non_credit_card_fraud_some_money_not_rec.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

estimated_net_consumer_loss.unit: US dollars estimated borne directly by consumers

spent_ten_or_more_hours_recovering_or_de.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud, approximate

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2024 SHED weighted survey estimates; overlapping fraud categories are preserved, and loss/recovery measures are conditional on non-credit-card fraud.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported survey estimates measure the most recent non-credit-card incident for relevant questions; the publication does not establish verified fraud, complete population incidence, exact event-level recovery, or causal effects.
observations.subgroup: All adult respondents; credit-card and other-fraud categories are not mutually exclusive.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credit-card consumer-liability protections may limit direct loss for many cases; category overlap, recall, reporting, and undercoverage can affect the exposure and dollar estimates.

denominator.unit: published age bands in the accessible Figure 30 table

median_pre_recovery_loss_age_18_44.unit: US dollars among adults with non-credit-card loss, before recovery

median_pre_recovery_loss_age_60_plus.unit: US dollars among adults with non-credit-card loss, before recovery

observations.method: Published age-conditioned SHED Figure 30 and Table 36 comparisons; incidence and conditional severity are kept as separate measures.
observations.uncertainty: Age-conditioned shares and medians describe survey respondents in the relevant conditional universes, not age-specific population risk, total losses, or digital-skill effects.
observations.subgroup: Adults ages 18–29, 30–44, 45–59, and 60+ for incidence; ages 18–44, 45–59, and 60+ for pre-recovery loss distribution.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher older-adult losses may partly reflect greater assets or different scam mix and do not by themselves establish greater vulnerability or weaker recovery.

related_sources.claim: FTC administrative reports provide a separate reported-loss and report-volume frame for comparison.
related_sources.access_boundary: FTC reports and the Federal Reserve survey use different units, coverage, definitions, and underreporting assumptions; they must not be pooled.

related_sources.claim: CFPB complaint records provide a separate institutional-response route frame.
related_sources.access_boundary: Complaint records are not the same people or denominator as SHED fraud respondents and do not establish remedy adequacy.

boundary: This record establishes survey-reported fraud exposure, conditional loss, recovery, and time-cost measures. It does not establish verified prevalence, firm liability, remedy adequacy, later trust, financial exit, political action, or a causal consumer-protection effect.
